2. Valves to renew = 180 sections * 4 valves per section = 720 valves
3. Crew days = 180 sections / 18 sections per day = 10 days

tasks.correctedLine: 2. Valves to renew = 180 sections * 3 valves per section = 540 valves
tasks.explanation: Line 2 used 4 valves instead of the stated 3 valves for valves per section. The correct calculation is Valves to renew = 180 sections * 3 valves per section = 540 valves.

tasks.prompt: Find the first wrong line in this renewal program quantity calculation for a system near Kelowna, British Columbia.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional renewal program near Kelowna, British Columbia: total mains length = 160 km, planned renewal share = 25 percent, given density = 38 service connections per km renewed and 6 valves per km renewed.

lines.label: 1. Length to renew = 160 km * 30 percent / 100 = 48 km
2. Services to renew = 48 km * 38 services per km = 1824 services
3. Valves to renew = 48 km * 6 valves per km = 288 valves

tasks.correctedLine: 1. Length to renew = 160 km * 25 percent / 100 = 40 km
tasks.explanation: Line 1 used 30 percent instead of the stated 25 percent for renewal share. The correct calculation is Length to renew = 160 km * 25 percent / 100 = 40 km.

tasks.prompt: Find the first wrong line in this watermain renewal quantity calculation for a capital program near Kamloops, British Columbia.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional renewal program near Kamloops, British Columbia: total mains length = 240 km, planned renewal share = 35 percent of total length, pipe is supplied in 6 m lengths, 1000 m = 1 km.

lines.label: 1. Total mains = 240 km * 1000 m/km = 240000 m
2. Renewal length = 240000 m * 35 percent / 100 = 84000 m
3. Pipe lengths needed = 84000 m / 6 m per length = 14500 lengths

tasks.correctedLine: 3. Pipe lengths needed = 84000 m / 6 m per length = 14000 lengths
tasks.explanation: Line 3 arithmetic is wrong. The correct calculation is Pipe lengths needed = 84000 m / 6 m per length = 14000 lengths.

tasks.prompt: Find the first wrong line in this renewal section quantity calculation for a program near Prince George, British Columbia.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional renewal program near Prince George, British Columbia: length to renew = 5600 m, standard section length = 28 m, valves renewed = 2 per section, crew production = 20 sections per day.

lines.label: 1. Sections to renew = 5600 m / 28 m per section = 200 sections
2. Valves to renew = 200 sections * 2 valves per section = 410 valves
3. Crew days = 200 sections / 20 sections per day = 10 days

tasks.correctedLine: 2. Valves to renew = 200 sections * 2 valves per section = 400 valves
tasks.explanation: Line 2 arithmetic is wrong. The correct calculation is Valves to renew = 200 sections * 2 valves per section = 400 valves.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building a five year water loss reduction strategy for a prairie city utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: utility wide strategy, from baseline audit to the approved five year targets.

cards.label: Complete a validated system water audit to establish the baseline loss volumes
Separate real losses from apparent losses and rank each component by volume
Set staged annual reduction targets for the largest loss components
Cost the intervention options for each target and rank them by volume saved per dollar
Assign program owners and annual budgets for the selected interventions
Present the strategy to utility leadership for approval and public reporting

tasks.explanation: A strategy built on a validated baseline can be measured year by year. Separating real and apparent losses prevents field crews chasing metering problems, and staged targets with owners and budgets turn the strategy into funded work.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for validating the data before a formal water loss audit is calculated.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: data validation stage for one audit year in a multi zone system.

cards.label: Verify production meter calibration records for every source entering the system
Reconcile production totals with treatment plant and pump station logs
Check billing extracts for missing accounts, estimated reads and zero reads
Confirm authorized unbilled volumes are supported by work records
Grade each audit input for confidence and record the grading basis
Lock the validated data set and calculate the audit from it only

tasks.explanation: An audit is only as good as its inputs. Production and billing data are proven first, confidence grading shows where the result is soft, and locking the data set prevents the audit changing as it is debated.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a component analysis of real losses across a large system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: background leakage, reported bursts and unreported leakage for the whole network.

cards.label: Total real losses from the validated audit for the study year
Estimate background leakage from pipe age, material and pressure data
Total reported burst volumes from break records and repair durations
Derive unreported leakage as the remainder after background and burst volumes
Compare each component with pressure and break history to test plausibility
Rank components and direct the next detection investment at the largest

tasks.explanation: Component analysis shows where real losses actually sit. Background, burst and unreported volumes are estimated in turn, the remainder is derived rather than guessed, and investment follows the largest proven component.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for an economic level of leakage study for utility leadership.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: study to find the loss level where further control costs more than the water saved.

cards.label: Confirm the current real loss volume and its trend from recent audits
Value saved water using production cost and the cost of new supply capacity
Price active leakage control options at increasing levels of effort
Find the point where the next unit of control costs more than the water it saves
Test the result against drought risk and supply security needs
Report the economic level and the recommended operating target to leadership

tasks.explanation: The economic level balances control cost against water value, including avoided capacity. Security needs can justify going beyond the pure economic point, but the decision is made openly with both numbers in front of leadership.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for prioritizing district metered areas across a whole city for loss work.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: portfolio ranking of forty districts for the next three years of detection work.

cards.label: Compile night flow, leakage rate and break history for every district
Normalize leakage by main length and by connection count for fair comparison
Score each district for loss volume, trend and consequence of failure
Group districts into annual work tranches that match crew capacity
Schedule the highest scoring districts in the first tranche
Review the ranking each year with new night flow data before committing the next tranche

tasks.explanation: Fair comparison needs normalized rates, not raw volumes that favour large districts. Scoring by volume, trend and consequence sends crews where loss and risk combine, and annual review keeps the portfolio honest as conditions change.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a pressure and leakage relationship study before a pressure program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one high pressure district where leakage falls at night are suspected.

cards.label: Log district inlet flow and pressure together over several weeks
Calculate night leakage at the recorded range of night pressures
Compare leakage change with pressure change to estimate the pressure sensitivity
Model leakage at candidate lower night pressures using the measured sensitivity
Check fire flow and customer minimum pressures at the candidate settings
Recommend the pressure setting that saves leakage without breaching service levels

tasks.explanation: Leakage responds to pressure, but the size of the response must be measured in the district itself. Modelling from measured sensitivity, then checking fire flow and minimum pressures, gives a setting that saves water without trading away service.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for an apparent loss reduction strategy at system scale.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy covering metering, billing and unauthorized use for the whole utility.

cards.label: Quantify apparent losses from the audit and split them by cause
Rank causes by volume, covering meter under registration, data errors and unauthorized use
Design a meter renewal and testing program aimed at the largest meter losses
Design billing data checks that catch transfer and estimation errors early
Set a hydrant permit and enforcement routine for unauthorized use
Track apparent loss recovery in the next audit and report the change

tasks.explanation: Apparent losses are recovered in offices and meter shops, not in trenches. Ranking by cause directs meter and data work at the biggest volumes first, and the next audit proves whether the recovery is real.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a system wide customer meter renewal strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: renewal strategy for all small customer meters over a ten year horizon.

cards.label: Analyse meter age, test accuracy by age band and consumption by class
Identify the age where accuracy loss makes renewal pay back fastest
Group meters into renewal cohorts by age, route and meter size
Set annual renewal volumes that match shop and field capacity
Plan billing notices and access arrangements for each cohort
Measure recovered consumption after each cohort and adjust the renewal age if needed

tasks.explanation: Renewal pays when accuracy loss is proven by age band testing, not by calendar habit. Cohorts matched to capacity keep the program deliverable, and measuring recovered consumption after each cohort refines the economic age for the next round.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a proactive hidden leak detection program using permanent noise loggers.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: logger deployment across the highest loss districts of a large city.

cards.label: Select districts and streets for logger coverage from the loss ranking
Deploy loggers on fittings at the planned spacing and record each location
Collect nightly noise data and flag fittings with sustained leak noise
Correlate flagged clusters to pinpoint the leak position before digging
Raise repair orders for pinpointed leaks in priority order
Review logger data after repairs to confirm noise has cleared and savings hold

tasks.explanation: Permanent loggers find leaks that sounding visits miss between surveys. Correlation before excavation avoids dry holes, and post repair review confirms the noise and the loss are both gone.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a burst frequency analysis to guide mains renewal.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: ten years of break records for the whole network.

cards.label: Clean the break database so each record carries pipe age, material, size and cause
Group breaks by pipe cohort and calculate breaks per kilometre per year
Compare cohorts to find the materials and ages failing fastest
Overlay break clusters with soil, pressure and frost depth information
Rank renewal candidates by break rate and consequence of failure
Feed the ranked list into the capital renewal program for costing

tasks.explanation: Break records only guide renewal once they are grouped into comparable cohorts. Rates per kilometre expose the failing materials, overlays explain why, and ranking by rate and consequence sends capital to the pipes most likely to fail next.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing cold climate design standards for new mains and services.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: standards review covering depth of bury, insulation and material choices.

cards.label: Compile failure data for shallow or poorly insulated installations
Compare current depth standards with measured maximum frost depths
Review insulation practice where depth cannot be achieved in rock or high water table areas
Update the standards with the frost evidence and the approved insulation details
Brief designers, inspectors and developers on the revised standards
Audit the first construction season under the new standards for compliance

tasks.explanation: Design standards must be set by measured frost, not by tradition. Failure data and frost records justify deeper bury or proper insulation, the revision is briefed to everyone who builds, and a first season audit makes the new standard real.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the annual water audit cycle at a Class 3 utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: recurring yearly cycle, from data close to published results.

cards.label: Close the audit year and freeze production and billing data extracts
Validate the extracts and grade input confidence with the audit team
Calculate the water balance and loss components for the year
Compare results with targets and with the previous three years
Brief utility leadership on variances and the causes found
Publish the audit summary and set the next year intervention priorities

tasks.explanation: A fixed annual cycle makes audits comparable across years. Freezing and validating data first prevents moving targets, multi year comparison separates trend from noise, and published results with priorities close the loop into action.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the business case for a major leakage intervention program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: business case for a three year district renewal and pressure program.

cards.label: State the loss volume the program will address from the validated audit
Forecast savings by year using measured district results, not vendor claims
Cost capital, operating and staffing needs for the full program life
Compare program cost with the value of water and capacity saved
Assess risks, including construction disruption and savings shortfall
Present the case with a recommendation and a savings verification plan

tasks.explanation: A credible case rests on the utility own measured savings, not supplier promises. Full life costing and an honest risk section let leadership judge the program, and a verification plan commits the program to proving its savings.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for using advanced metering data in the loss program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: new hourly customer meter data feeding district balances in a large system.

cards.label: Confirm district boundaries align with the meter data grouping
Aggregate hourly customer consumption to district level for each night
Compare district metered consumption with district inlet flow for the same nights
Flag districts where the gap grows, showing rising unaccounted use
Investigate flagged districts for leakage, theft or meter data faults
Add the district gap trend to the monthly loss dashboard for leadership

tasks.explanation: Hourly meter data turns the district balance from an annual estimate into a monthly signal. Comparing consumption with inlet flow on the same nights isolates the gap, and trending it monthly catches new losses while they are small.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing winter losses after a severe cold period in a northern city.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: post winter review covering frost related bursts and running water bleeds.

cards.label: Total winter burst repairs and compare with the five year winter average
Total bleed water volumes authorized to protect frozen services
Separate frost depth driven failures from age driven failures in the records
Review which mains and services failed repeatedly at shallow depth
Rank depth and insulation corrections for the summer construction season
Report winter loss costs and the correction plan to leadership

tasks.explanation: Winter losses mix frost effects with normal aging, and the review must separate them. Bleed volumes are counted honestly as loss, repeat shallow failures are ranked for correction in summer, and leadership sees the full winter cost.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for briefing senior leadership to set the utility loss target.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one decision briefing for the annual target in a multi zone utility.

cards.label: Prepare the audit trend, component split and peer utility comparison
Prepare costed options for holding, reducing moderately and reducing aggressively
Show the service and supply risks of each option in plain terms
Record the target leadership selects and the reasons given
Translate the target into district and program level sub targets
Schedule the mid year progress review against the selected target

tasks.explanation: Leadership can only set a defensible target when options carry costs and risks together. Recording the reasons protects the target from later revision, and sub targets plus a mid year review keep the commitment managed.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the base year demand model for a twenty year forecast.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: base year construction for a growing western city system.

cards.label: Select a weather normal base year and document why it represents typical demand
Total base year production and split it by customer class from billing data
Separate billed consumption, authorized unbilled use and losses
Calculate per capita and per connection use for each customer class
Check the base year against the previous five years for anomalies
Lock the base year data set as the foundation of the forecast

tasks.explanation: Every forecast inherits the errors of its base year. A weather normal year, split by class with losses separated, gives unit demands that can be projected, and locking the set keeps later debate about method rather than data.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building population and growth scenarios for demand forecasting.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: low, expected and high growth scenarios for a twenty year horizon.

cards.label: Obtain official population and development projections for the service area
Translate projections into serviced connections by district and by phase
Build low, expected and high scenarios with stated assumptions for each
Apply unit demands by customer class to each scenario
Compare scenario demands with current system capacity by district
Carry all three scenarios into capacity planning so triggers, not dates, drive projects

tasks.explanation: Scenarios protect the utility from betting the capital plan on one growth guess. Translating population into phased connections by district shows where growth lands, and trigger based planning builds capacity when growth proves itself.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing peaking factors used in capacity planning.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review of maximum day and peak hour factors from ten years of records.

cards.label: Extract maximum day and peak hour demands for each of the past ten years
Relate each peak to weather, restrictions and major customer use in that year
Remove peaks caused by one time events that planning should not design for
Calculate the planning peaking factors from the remaining record
Compare the factors with the values in the current master plan
Update the master plan factors and record the evidence for the change

tasks.explanation: Peaking factors set the size of everything the utility builds. Peaks are explained before they are averaged, one time events are excluded openly, and the master plan is updated from evidence so designs stay defensible.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for adjusting the demand forecast for a hotter, drier climate trend.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: forecast adjustment for summer irrigation demand in a prairie system.

cards.label: Analyse summer demand against temperature and rainfall over twenty years
Estimate the demand change per degree of summer temperature from the record
Apply the climate trend for the forecast horizon to the summer component only
Test the adjusted peak against storage and pumping capacity
Identify the year the adjusted peak first exceeds firm capacity
Report the climate adjusted capacity trigger year to leadership

tasks.explanation: Climate effects belong on the weather sensitive summer component, not smeared across all demand. The measured temperature response drives the adjustment, and the output leadership needs is the year firm capacity is first exceeded.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for updating the distribution master plan.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: full master plan update for a city expecting major growth.

cards.label: Refresh the demand forecast with the latest base year and growth scenarios
Update the hydraulic model with current network and operations data
Test the model against forecast demands for each planning horizon
List capacity deficiencies by zone, year and growth scenario
Develop project options that resolve each deficiency with trigger years
Present the updated plan and project triggers to leadership for adoption

tasks.explanation: The master plan links forecast, model and projects in that order. Deficiencies are located by zone and scenario before options are drawn, and adoption of triggers rather than fixed dates keeps the plan useful as growth changes pace.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for assessing whether system storage is adequate for the next decade.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: storage assessment covering balancing, fire and emergency volumes.

cards.label: Calculate current balancing storage need from the diurnal demand pattern
Add the fire storage requirement for the largest risk area served
Add the emergency storage allowance set by utility policy
Compare the total need with usable storage by zone, not just system wide
Forecast the need at five and ten years using the demand scenarios
Recommend storage projects with trigger years where zone deficits appear

tasks.explanation: Storage adequacy is a zone question, because water stored across town cannot serve a local peak. Balancing, fire and emergency needs are stacked openly, and zone deficits with trigger years become the storage program.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a pump station firm capacity review across all stations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review triggered by forecast growth in the upper zones.

cards.label: List each station duty pumps, standby pumps and rated capacities
Define firm capacity as output with the largest pump out of service
Compare firm capacity with current and forecast zone peak demands
Field test the oldest stations to confirm rated output is still achieved
Rank stations by the year firm capacity is exceeded
Program upgrades in rank order with design starting ahead of the trigger year

tasks.explanation: Firm capacity, with the largest unit out, is the honest measure of a station. Field testing catches derated pumps that paper ratings hide, and ranking by exceedance year sequences upgrades before growth exposes the gap.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for checking capacity for a major new development application.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one large subdivision and commercial development at the city edge.

cards.label: Obtain the development phasing, unit counts and proposed demands
Add the phased demands to the hydraulic model at the proposed connection points
Test peak hour pressures and fire flow at the development under full build out
Identify off site upgrades the development triggers on existing mains
Set the upgrade and cost sharing conditions in the servicing response
Record the committed demands in the forecast so later applications see them

tasks.explanation: Each major application must be tested at full build out, not first phase only. Off site effects are identified while conditions can still be set, and recording committed demand prevents the same capacity being promised twice.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the demand management stages of a drought plan.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: staged restrictions plan for a system supplied by a snowmelt river.

cards.label: Define drought trigger levels from source storage and river flow indicators
Estimate the demand saving each restriction stage must deliver
Match measures to stages, from voluntary savings to mandatory limits
Confirm enforcement, communications and exemption routines for each stage
Test the staged savings against the worst recorded drought demand pattern
Approve the plan and pre draft public notices for each stage

tasks.explanation: Drought stages must be tied to measurable source triggers, not to judgement in a crisis. Savings are estimated per stage and tested against the worst recorded pattern, and pre drafted notices let the utility act the day a trigger is reached.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing forecast accuracy five years into a master plan.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: mid plan review comparing forecast demands with actual demands.

cards.label: Extract actual production and connections for the five years since the forecast
Compare actuals with each growth scenario year by year
Identify which scenario tracked reality and where class demands diverged
Explain divergences from development records and weather data
Rebase the forecast on the tracking scenario with corrected unit demands
Report whether project triggers move earlier or later as a result

tasks.explanation: A forecast review is an audit of the utility own assumptions. Tracking which scenario matched reality shows whether growth or unit demand was misjudged, and rebasing moves project triggers honestly in either direction.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for planning service for a large new industrial water customer.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: one food processing plant proposing high steady demand with peak batches.

cards.label: Obtain the customer process demand profile, peaks and quality needs
Check average and peak effects on the supplying zone and storage
Confirm backflow protection and any pretreatment conditions for the connection
Agree demand charges, peak limits and curtailment terms for drought stages
Design the metering and monitoring for the service with the customer
Add the committed profile to the demand forecast and zone records

tasks.explanation: A large steady customer changes zone behaviour every day, not just at peak. Peak and drought terms are agreed before connection, monitoring is designed in from the start, and the forecast carries the real profile rather than an average.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for planning fire flow upgrades across older districts.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: city wide fire flow deficiency program for pre war neighbourhoods.

cards.label: Compile hydrant test results and model estimates for every older district
Rank streets by the gap between available flow and the protection need
Group deficient streets into renewal areas that share undersized mains
Sequence areas by risk, combining fire flow with break history
Cost the grouped program and phase it across the capital plan years
Retest each completed area and publish the improved flow results

tasks.explanation: Fire flow work grouped by shared mains fixes whole areas at once instead of scattering hydrant by hydrant. Combining flow gaps with break history spends once on streets that need renewal anyway, and retesting proves the protection gained.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for planning an emergency intertie with a neighbouring utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: intertie study between two prairie cities sharing a regional supply risk.

cards.label: Define the emergency scenarios the intertie must cover and their durations
Estimate the flow each city must be able to send and receive in each scenario
Locate connection points where pressures can be matched or boosted
Agree water quality, metering and cost sharing terms in principle
Design the connection works and the operating procedure for activation
Exercise the intertie annually and review the agreement after each use

tasks.explanation: An intertie is an operating agreement as much as a pipe. Scenarios size the flows, pressure and quality terms are settled before construction, and annual exercising keeps the connection and the relationship ready for the real event.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for rebuilding the distribution asset inventory to decision grade.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: inventory rebuild for mains, valves, hydrants and services in a large system.

cards.label: Define the asset attributes the renewal decisions actually require
Extract existing records and grade each attribute for completeness
Field verify a sample of records in each district to measure error rates
Correct systematic errors found in the sample across the full data set
Set update routines so new works enter the inventory at commissioning
Report inventory confidence by asset class to the asset management team

tasks.explanation: Decision grade data starts from the decisions, not from what the old database happens to hold. Sample verification measures real error rates, systematic faults are fixed at scale, and commissioning updates stop the inventory decaying again.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a condition assessment program for critical large mains.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: trunk mains whose failure would cut supply to whole zones.

cards.label: Rank trunk mains by consequence of failure to select assessment candidates
Choose assessment methods matched to pipe material and access
Plan outages and bypass supply for each assessment window
Carry out the assessments and record defects in the standard format
Convert findings into remaining life estimates for each main
Feed the results into renewal timing and interim risk controls

tasks.explanation: Assessment money goes first where failure hurts most. Methods must fit the pipe, bypass planning keeps customers supplied during the work, and findings only matter once they become remaining life estimates that move renewal decisions.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the distribution asset risk register.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: register covering likelihood and consequence for all major asset classes.

cards.label: List failure modes for each asset class with operations and maintenance staff
Score likelihood from break, failure and condition records
Score consequence for customers, water quality, cost and reputation
Plot assets on the risk matrix and identify the highest risk group
Assign a treatment, owner and review date to every high risk entry
Review the register quarterly and after every major failure

tasks.explanation: A register built with field staff captures the failure modes records miss. Likelihood from evidence and consequence across four dimensions give a defensible ranking, and owners with review dates keep high risks actively treated.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting up the mains renewal prioritization model.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: model combining break history, condition, risk and coordination factors.

cards.label: Select the factors the model will score, with weights agreed by leadership
Assemble clean data for every factor at individual pipe segment level
Run the model and produce the first ranked renewal list
Field check the top ranked segments for data errors and local knowledge
Adjust weights only where the field check shows a systematic bias
Publish the ranked list as the basis of the five year renewal program

tasks.explanation: Weights are a leadership decision made before results are seen, which keeps the model honest. Field checking the top of the list catches data errors where they matter most, and weight changes need evidence of bias, not disappointment with the ranking.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the ten year distribution capital plan.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: plan covering renewal, growth, quality and compliance projects.

cards.label: Collect project needs from renewal, capacity, quality and risk programs
Scope and cost each project at planning level with stated confidence
Sequence projects by trigger year, risk and construction coordination
Balance annual spending against the funding the utility can sustain
Identify the risk carried by any project deferred beyond its trigger
Present the balanced plan with deferral risks to leadership for approval

tasks.explanation: A capital plan is a balancing act made visible. Needs from every program compete in one list, sequencing respects triggers and coordination, and deferral risks are stated openly so approval is a real choice.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a system wide valve program strategy review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy for critical valve exercising, repair and replacement.

cards.label: Identify critical valves whose failure would extend an outage area
Review exercising completion and failure records for the critical set
Set exercising frequencies by criticality rather than one interval for all
Program replacements for valves that fail exercising twice
Stock the repair parts the failure records show are actually needed
Report valve readiness for the largest isolation areas to leadership

tasks.explanation: Not all valves matter equally in an emergency. Criticality sets the exercising rhythm, repeat failures earn replacement rather than another note, and readiness reporting focuses on the isolations leadership will ask about after the next big break.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reviewing the hydrant inspection and flow testing strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy covering all hydrants in a cold climate city.

cards.label: Review inspection findings for the most common hydrant defects by age and make
Set flow testing coverage so every hydrant is tested within the policy cycle
Add winter checks for drainage and freeze damage in problem areas
Program repairs by defect severity, with out of service hydrants first
Record flow results into the fire flow planning data set
Report hydrant availability to the fire department each year

tasks.explanation: Hydrant strategy links maintenance to fire protection outcomes. Defect patterns by make guide purchasing, winter drainage checks prevent freeze failures, and flow data flows straight into the planning set the fire department shares.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a service line renewal program targeting repeat freeze and leak failures.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program for services with repeated winter failures in older districts.

cards.label: Extract services with two or more freeze or leak repairs in five years
Group the repeat failures by street to find shared depth or material causes
Inspect a sample of grouped services to confirm the cause before designing
Design street by street renewal with corrected depth and material
Schedule renewals in the frost free construction season by group priority
Track the renewed streets through the next two winters for failure recurrence

tasks.explanation: Repeat failures at the same services signal a design fault, not bad luck. Grouping by street exposes shared causes, renewal corrects depth and material together, and two winters of tracking prove the fix before the program scales.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the storage reservoir inspection and cleaning program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program covering all ground reservoirs and elevated tanks.

cards.label: Set inspection intervals by tank age, coating condition and water quality history
Plan each inspection with isolation, bypass supply and confined space controls
Inspect structure, coating, vents, screens and security during the outage
Sample sediment and review water quality results from the tank
Complete repairs and recoating decisions from the findings before refilling
Return the tank to service with disinfection and sampling as procedure requires

tasks.explanation: Tank outages are rare, so each one must answer structure, coating, security and quality questions together. Findings are acted on before refilling because the next chance may be years away, and return to service follows the full disinfection routine.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for pump station renewal planning across the station fleet.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: fleet plan for stations aged twenty to forty years.

cards.label: Compile station age, run hours, failure history and parts availability
Assess each station for capacity, reliability and energy performance
Identify stations where parts obsolescence creates an urgent risk
Sequence renewals so no zone depends on two stations under renewal at once
Stage design work to finish one year ahead of each construction window
Present the fleet plan with the risk of the current sequence to leadership

tasks.explanation: Fleet planning prevents several stations failing into the same decade. Obsolescence can outrank age as a risk, sequencing protects zone redundancy, and design lead time is planned so construction windows are never wasted waiting for drawings.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building a break prediction review to target inspections.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual prediction cycle using break, soil, pressure and age data.

cards.label: Assemble the updated break history and asset data for the model run
Run the prediction and list segments with the highest failure probability
Compare predictions with the breaks that actually occurred last year
Investigate the largest misses to find missing or wrong input data
Correct the data faults and rerun the prediction for this year
Issue the corrected high probability list to inspection and renewal teams

tasks.explanation: A prediction model earns trust by being scored against last year breaks. Misses are treated as data problems first, which improves both the model and the inventory, and only the corrected list goes to the field teams.
